The calculation of the overall response probability entails a sum over the four scenarios weighted by their probabilities. The EPF model has 3 parameters (Table 1): J1 , α, and K. The VPF model has 4 parameters: J1 , τ , α, and K. Model fitting and model comparison follow the same procedures as described above.

Model Fits

Our goal was to assess which model best describes search in VWM, and whether that description is good. In model comparison according to AIC, BIC, and cross-validation, we found consistently that the best-fitting model was the VP model, and that adding an item limit did not improve the fit (Fig. 5, Fig. A2). In terms of the visual goodness of fit, we expect the EPF and VPF models to fit at least as well as the EP and VP models, and they do (Fig. 4). The VP and VPF models both provide a visibly excellent fit to the data. The EPF model fits visibly better than the EP model, but these two models ultimately do slightly worse than the VP and VPF models.

In the VP model, we estimated the parameter log α as 0.508 ± 0.084, with α describing the decrease of mean precision with set size. All parameter estimates can be found in Table A1 (but with the logarithm taken before averaging).

We subsequently verified that model comparisons among the VP, VPF, EP, and EPF models were meaningful.

Specifically, we tested whether EPF, rather than VP, emerged as the best-fitting model when the data were generated by EPF. We focused on EPF because it provides the starkest contrast to VP. We generated 100 datasets using actual stimulus values from our experimental data, and then simulated the responses from the EPF parameters. For each simulated participant, J, α, and K were drawn uniformly from the full ranges obtained through model fitting. EPF was indeed the best-performing model for these simulated datasets (Fig. Appendix 6). Thus, VP's better fit to the observed data is not inevitable.

Thus far, the decision rule specified in our modeling methodology assumes that the observers have access to the specific precision with which the stimulus was encoded. Relying on a decision rule in which the observer has access to the specific precisions with which the stimuli are encoded has been a common and successful assumption in theories of cue combination (Serwe, Körding, & Trommershäuser, 2011) and other forms of probabilistic computation (Adler & Ma, 2018; Ma et al., 2011; Qamar et al., 2013; Denison, Adler, Carrasco, & Ma, 2018). There is also substantial evidence for this within working memory (Keshvari et al., 2012; M. Honig, Ma, & Fougnie, 2020): the best-performing models are ones in which not only is encoding precision variable across stimuli and trials, but the observer also takes these variations into account. To examine the impact of this decision rule selection, we tested the VP model with a suboptimal decision rule in which the observer does not have access to precision and assumes that the precision is the same for all items. Instead, the observer simply reports the location where the measured color (x 1 or x 2 ) is closest (in a circular sense) to the target color, s T . We find that the VP model with the optimal decision rule outperforms the VP model with the suboptimal decision rule according to AIC, BIC, and visual goodness of fit (Figure A1). Target Confusability Competition model

An alternative model for working memory is the Target Confusability Competition (TCC) model (Schurgin et al., 2020).

For color, its starting point is that distances in CIELAB color space map nonlinearly to psychological distances. The TCC model consists of two steps (Figure 7A). First, the model describes the discriminability (d ′ ) of a pair of stimuli as a function of their color distance. Then, it maps this d ′ to proportion correct in a particular task. The first step is task-independent and specific to the TCC model, while the second step is task-dependent and determined by signal detection theory (SDT).

Computing d ′ . In the TCC framework, a memory-based decision is made by comparing noisy memories x i of true stimulus values s i ; the noise is assumed to be Gaussian. When the observer encodes N stimuli, the discriminability d ′ of two stimuli that are a distance ∆s apart is assumed to be given by where Sim(∆s) is a psychological similarity function that depends only on ∆s, and d ′ scale (N ) is a scaling factor that only depends on N .

In other words, across set sizes, the d ′ (∆s) curves have the same shape and differ only by a fitted scaling factor (Figure 7B). The similarity function is empirically measured in a given domain and is expected to decrease monotonically.

From d' to p correct . The second step involves mapping d ′ to proportion correct within a given task. This mapping is provided by signal detection theory and is not specific to the TCC model. Here, we derive this mapping for our task, in which the participant reports which of two locations contained a target color. On each trial, the target color s 1 is encoded as a noisy memory x 1 and the non-target color s 2 is encoded as a noisy memory x 2 . SDT assumes that x 1 and x 2 follow Gaussian distributions. Without loss of generality, we set the target value to s1 = 0 and the standard deviation of the Gaussian noise to 1. Then, the distribution of the target memory is centered at 0 and that of the non-target memory at d ′ :

In our task, the observer knows the target color and compares it to the two noisy memories, x 1 and x 2 , which correspond to the two response alternatives. The optimal response is the location containing the memory that is closest to 0. Due to noise, this response may be incorrect. The probability of a correct response is the probability that the memory from the target location is closest to 0:

We will refer to this mapping as f (d ′ ). This function increases monotonically with increasing d ′ , as the discriminability between x 1 and x 2 increases (Figure 7C). For a given value of d ′ , we approximated this probability using Monte Carlo simulation with 200,000 sampled (x 1 , x 2 ) pairs.

From d ′ to p correct in the TCC model. By combining Equations ( 23) and ( 26), we obtain probability correct as a function of ∆s and N . On each trial, we calculated d ′ from Equation ( 23) using the numerical form of Sim provided by Schurgin et al. (2020) and then approximated Equation ( 26) using Monte Carlo simulation. The free parameters in the resulting TCC model for this experiment are d ′ scale for each set size ∈ {2, 4, 6, 8}. For each participant and set size N , we estimated the corresponding free parameter through maximum-likelihood estimation.

Model Fits We found that the fits of the TCC model were overall good, but slightly worse than those of our best-fitting VP model (Figure 8). The TCC model had a higher AIC (∆AIC = 220, 95% CI = [120, 340]) and BIC (∆ BIC = 280, 95% CI = [180, 350]) than the VP model, indicating that the VP model provided a consistently better fit to the data, even after penalizing for model complexity.

Fitting the resource-rational models

While the non-parametric VP model had parameters J2 , J4 , J6 , and J8 , mean precision in the VP-RR models is not fitted to the data but internally derived by the observer. The VP-RR model with linear resource cost has two free parameters, λ and τ , whereas the VP-RR model with power law resource cost has an additional parameter β. We again fitted these parameters using BADS, using a logarithmic transformation for λ and τ . We chose the plausible ranges to be [-12, -1] for log λ, [log(0.05), log(600)] for log τ , and [-3, 3] for log β.

Model Fits

The VP-RR model with a linear cost function does not capture the data well and is visibly inferior to the VP and the VP non-parametric models. This is quantitatively confirmed with an AIC and BIC model comparison as the VP-RR model with the linear resource cost is worse than the VP model according to AIC but indistinguishable by BIC metrics (Fig. 12A,B). However, the VP-RR model with a power law cost fits qualitatively and quantitatively better than the linear-cost model (Figs. 11, 12), and is indistinguishable from the VP model in model comparison; AIC and BIC produce the same result in this case, because the models both have 3 parameters (Fig. 12). The relationship between mean precision and set size that is internally derived in the VP-RR model with power law resource cost is very similar to the fitted relationships that we previously found in the VP and VP Non-parametric models (Fig. 12C).

Discussion

In this paper, we take a principled modeling approach to search in VWM. Our main findings are threefold. First, several Bayesian observer models accounted for behavior in this task reasonably well, showing that computational frameworks from visual search and VWM extend naturally to search in VWM. Second, the variable-precision (VP) model provided the best overall account of behavior, even after penalizing for model complexity, with no need for assuming additional item limits. These results fit with previous work on resource limitations in visual search (Mazyar et al., 2012; Mihali & Ma, 2020) and visual working memory (Ma et al., 2014; Bays & Husain, 2008; Fougnie et al., 2012; Mazyar et al., 2012; Mazyar, van den Berg, Seilheimer, & Ma, 2013; van den Berg et al., 2012; D. T. Devkar et al., 2015; Bays, Schneegans, Ma, & Brady, 2024). More broadly, our results show that a Bayesian observer framework in which precision decreases with set size extends naturally to search in VWM. Interestingly, we also found that the Target Confusability Competition (TCC) model produced very similar predictions to those of the VP model despite its different modeling assumptions. Third, a resource-rational modeling approach, which derived encoding precision from a trade-off between neural and behavioral cost, was unable to outperform the VP model. To reach these conclusions, we applied computational approaches from visual search and VWM to a new memory-based localization task. We tested Bayesian observer models with different encoding stages and decision rules, ranging from resource models to more normative resource-rational models that imposed stronger constraints on how an observer should allocate encoding resources. This comparison allowed us to ask not only which model fit behavior best, but also whether different theoretical modeling commitments actually lead to different empirical predictions.

Our comparison of the TCC model with our best-performing VP model opened a new avenue of exploration. We delved deeper into the differences between the TCC and VP models and asked what distinguishes them conceptually.

Although the two models appear to make different assumptions, we found that they arrive at very similar predictions. TCC makes psychophysical scaling explicit, whereas VP does not. However, in practice, the explicit psychophysical scaling in TCC appears to be implicitly approximated in VP through its assumption of circular color distance. Thus, despite their different formulations, the two models may capture similar underlying structure. Consistent with this idea, our reverse-engineering analysis showed that the VP model, re-expressed in terms of effective d ′ , produces discriminability patterns similar to those of the TCC model. A related question has been asked before in the context of a different resource model, the neural resource model (Bays, 2014) Bays (2019); Tomić and Bays (2024)argued that TCC and the neural resource model share a common underlying architecture. We were able to extend their hypothesis by comparing TCC with a different resource model, the VP model. Importantly, we compared them using proportion correct, a quantity that is well-defined across feature spaces, including the circular geometry of color spaces used in our task.

Next, we asked whether the observed precision patterns can also be explained as the result of a normative resourceallocation principle. To address this, we tested a resource-rational version of the VP model, in which encoding precision is derived from minimizing a combination of behavioral cost and neural cost. This model performed well, but only after adding an arbitrary power-law parameter to the resource cost function. The basic VP model, its non-parametric variant, and its best resource-rational variant all indicated a decrease in mean precision with set size that approximated a power law. At the same time, these results do not provide a strong test of the resource-rational framework in general. Adding the cost-function parameter effectively shifts flexibility from one power law governing precision to another power law governing cost. Stronger tests could be conducted in future work by including more set sizes or by obtaining an independent measure of the cost of precision.

Our results are qualitatively very similar to previous patterns established for search in perception (Kuo et al., 2009; Kong & Fougnie, 2019; Mihali & Ma, 2020). These studies showed that accuracy decreased with increasing set size and with increasing target-distractor similarity in both perception and memory. Our work approached the same question using precise psychophysical measurements and computational modeling. Measuring neural activity in both conditions could further refine this account. In delayed localization, Li, Sprague, Yoo, Ma, and Curtis (2021, 2025) showed that VWM content and uncertainty are jointly encoded in early visual cortex, and that neural activity during the delay period predicts behavioral performance. A natural extension would be to ask whether the same neural representations that support perceptual search also support search in VWM.

A related open question is whether search in VWM proceeds serially or in parallel. Previous work has suggested that response times increasing with set size imply serial scanning of memory, as in Sternberg (1966)'s classic detection task with discrete symbols. Our task shares the same basic structure-participants encode a set of items, then use a probe to search memory and make a binary response-and we too find that response times increase approximately linearly with set size (Appendix 5). However, Sternberg's paradigm used easily discriminable stimuli that minimized representational uncertainty, bringing them closer to investigating the temporal dynamics of retrieval. Our task uses continuous visual features, and performance depends not just on whether retrieval occurred but on the precision of noisy memory representations. Our models are built to capture this precision-dependent component, not retrieval speed.

The linear response time increase is therefore consistent with, but does not by itself imply, serial search. Distinguishing serial from parallel search in VWM would require paradigms that more directly target retrieval dynamics, for example by combining response time measurements with eye tracking or by manipulating the temporal structure of the search process.

Another possible future direction comes from the fact that here we have only approached one way in which visual search and VWM interact. Throughout, we have treated search in VWM as a self-contained task: an observer holds a set of items in memory and searches that memory for a match to an external probe. The reverse relationship also occurs during ordinary visual search of an external display, where an observer holds a target template in memory and uses it to guide search through the visual array. This is straightforward when the target is fixed, but becomes more demanding when the target varies from trial to trial (Chelazzi, Miller, Duncan, & Desimone, 1993; Carlisle, Arita, Pardo, & Woodman, 2011; Goldstein & Beck, 2018), or when irrelevant features of the target are encoded alongside the relevant one (Olivers, Peters, Houtkamp, & Roelfsema, 2011; Hollingworth & Beck, 2016; van Moorselaar, Theeuwes, & Olivers, 2014). In these cases, the precision with which the target template is maintained in memory should directly affect search performance, much as memory precision determined performance in our task. This suggests that the same computational framework used here, namely precision decreasing with set size and search performance governed by noisy memory representations, may extend to template-guided search as well.

Lastly, our experiment is simplified in several ways. First, it manipulates only two stimulus dimensions-location and color-and the range of variation within each dimension is limited. For example, stimuli can appear in only eight possible locations, all positioned at a fixed distance from the central fixation point. This limits the generalizability of our findings. One approach to increase ecological validity in experimental design would be to use more naturalistic stimuli such as real-world objects or photographs (Brady, Konkle, Gill, Oliva, & Alvarez, 2013; Bates, Lerch, Sims, & Jacobs, 2019), but doing so increases stimulus complexity while leaving the task structure largely unchanged. A second approach would be to increase the complexity of the task itself. In the real world, items may differ in value or behavioral relevance, and observers may combine perceptual and reward information to decide what to search for (Navalpakkam, Koch, Rangel, & Perona, 2010). Real search may also involve unpredictable item positions, visual clutter, and time pressure, none of which our paradigm imposed. Furthermore, real-world scenarios in which people search memory involve structured scenes rather than arbitrary arrays, bringing in semantic and spatial regularities that constrain where targets are likely to be found (Võ & Wolfe, 2015). Incorporating any of these elements into laboratory paradigms for search in VWM could make those paradigms more relevant to real-world search, and testing whether the computational models studied here generalize to these richer conditions would be a natural extension of this work.

Data and code availability

Data, analysis, and modeling code are provided at: https://github.com/WeiJiMaLab/Search-In-VWM

Conclusion

This work introduced a simple two-alternative forced-choice paradigm to measure search in visual working memory (VWM), and adapted existing computational frameworks from VWM and visual search to the resulting behavior. Our best-fitting model consisted of a variable precision encoding scheme and a Bayesian decision stage, with no benefit of adding an item limit. Applying the Target Confusability Competition model with its explicit incorporation of the psychophysical scaling framework did not provide a better fit to our data. Conceptually, we found that the VP framework and TCC framework have distinct but ultimately comparable ways of incorporating nonlinearities in stimulus distance. Lastly, a resource-rational variant of the VP model, in which mean precision was derived from a trade-off between behavioral and encoding cost, captured behavior well but did not outperform the standard VP model.

discriminability d ′ , as captured by the similarity function Sim (Equation 23; Figure 7B). The VP model, however, does not postulate such a function. How can it then still generate qualitatively similar fits and even perform quantitatively a little better than the TCC model? We claim that while the nonlinearity is not manually constructed in the VP model, it is implicitly present.

The central quantity in the TCC model is d ′ , which assumes Gaussian distributions over the internal representations of stimuli. While this is a common assumption in the psychophysics literature and could be justified if "internal representation" is defined sufficiently abstractly, it is not grounded in the physical stimulus space. In our task, as in the tasks used by Schurgin et al. (2020), color space is circular. However, the TCC model is a signal detection theory model and thus assumes Gaussian noise, which does not respect the circular geometry of color space. By contrast, in the VP model, measurement noise is defined directly in circular space (via the von Mises distribution). The circular nature of the space is carried through both the generative model and the (cosine-based) decision rule. Therefore, it is possible that in the VP model, a nonlinear relationship between stimulus distance and discriminability emerges without separately positing an explicit similarity mapping.

To show that this is indeed the case, we "reverse engineered" d ′ values from the VP model's predicted proportion correct per participant. Recall that we denoted by f (d ′ ) the mapping from d ′ to proportion correct in our task within an SDT framework (Equation 26). This mapping only depended on the task and on the basic SDT assumptions of Equations 24 and 25, and not on any of the specific assumptions of either the TCC or the VP model. We first calculated this mapping numerically for a fine grid of d ′ values ∈ [0, 8]; for each value of d ′ , we drew 200,000 samples of x 1 ∼ N (0, 1) and x 2 ∼ N (d ′ , 1), and calculated the proportion of these samples for which |x 2 | > |x 1 |. Then, for each combination of color distance, set size, and participant, we took proportion correct as predicted by the fitted VP model and converted it to a d ′ value using our numerical approximation to f and one-dimensional linear interpolation (MATLAB's interp1). The resulting values are interpretable as discriminability values, even though the concept of discriminability is not part of the VP model per se; therefore, we call it "effective discriminability" or "effective d ′ ."

As we hypothesized, we found that the VP model implicitly contains a nonlinear mapping between discriminability and color distance (Figure 9B). Moreover, the TCC and VP models yielded qualitatively similar d ′ patterns (Figure 9A vs B). However, under the VP model, the effective d ′ curves across set sizes were not simply scaled multiples of one another. This suggests that the scaling assumption built into the TCC model may be restrictive, potentially explaining why the TCC model fits the behavioral data slightly worse overall than the VP model.

While we compared the TCC model to the variable-precision model-a resource model-recent work compared it

to a different resource model-the neural resource model (Bays, 2019; Tomić & Bays, 2024). In this neural resource model of working memory (Bays, 2014), a population of independent Poisson neurons encodes a memorized stimulus, with gain inversely proportional to set size. The authors note that d ′ can be naturally derived from such a model.

To obtain the dependence of d ′ on set size, they further note that d ′ scales with the square root of neural gain and thus inversely with the square root of set size. To obtain the dependence of d ′ on stimulus distance, the authors use the von Mises tuning curve of a single neuron directly as the functional form. This is somewhat puzzling, because the discriminability of two stimuli based on a population is not identical to that based on a single neuron (Carney et al., 1989; Seung & Sompolinsky, 1993; Ma, 2010). To obtain the population-based discriminability, one would have to either simulate the neural responses to the stimulus pairs used in the experiment or use the (analytical) distribution of maximum-likelihood estimates of the stimuli based on the neural activity (Ma, 2010). The latter approach would reduce to our "reverse engineering" process, with our measurement x of a stimulus identified with the maximumlikelihood estimate of that stimulus based on the neural response, which is standard practice in population coding models (Ma, 2010). In either approach, it would be obvious that the decision is made in a circular space and therefore, the standard signal detection theory formalism and the standard definition of d ′ , which assume Gaussian noise on the real line, do not apply. It is exactly for this reason that in the VP model, we calculated proportion correct, which is well-defined in any space, and only reverse-engineered an effective d ′ to facilitate comparison with the TCC model.

In sum, the d ′ comparison between the TCC model and the neural resource model by Tomić and Bays (2024), if done correctly, would look very similar to the comparison between the TCC model and the VP model presented here.

Resource-rational models

Following van den Berg and Ma (2018), who found evidence for resource-rational behavior in some VWM tasks, we aim to understand whether behavior in search in VWM is also resource-rational. Observers might internally set their precision not only to maximize accuracy, but also to minimize the neural resources spent on encoding stimuli (Attwell & Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003; Griffiths et al., 2015). Specifically, we formulate resource-rational variants of the VP model (VP-RR models) and ask whether they can outperform the standard VP model.

Figure 2: Summary statistics.Proportion correct varied strongly with set size and color distance between the target and the non-target, but weakly with the spatial distance between them. (A) Proportion correct as a function of set size. (B) Proportion correct as a function of color distance. (C) Proportion correct as a function of spatial distance for each set size. While color distance and spatial distance are both measured in degrees, the two measures have different meanings. Color distance represents distance in CIELAB color space. Spatial distance represents circular distance on an imaginary circle centered at the screen's fixation point. One unit of spatial distance corresponds to 45 • of circular distance, corresponding to the case when the target and non-target are located adjacently.

Figure 3: Bayesian model of search in VWM. (A) Generative model. Each node represents a variable and each arrow represents a conditional dependence between variables. We denote by L the location of the target (1 or 2). T = (T1, T2) is a one-hot representation of target location: T = (1, 0) or T = (0, 1). We denote by si (and xi) the stimulus (memory) at location i (which is 1 or 2). (B) The Bayesian observer inverts the generative model, ultimately giving rise to a decision rule acting on a pair of memories (x1, x2). Each panel visualizes the decision rule for one possible combination of precision values for the two stimuli (J1 and J2). The observer reports target location 1 (white) or 2 (black).

3B 230 shows the decision landscapes for four combinations of precision values associated with the two memories. Generally 231 speaking, when a memory of a stimulus color is sufficiently close to the target color (the smaller the magnitude of 232 x i -s T is), its location gets chosen. However, the values of precision matter for the shape of the landscape. If the 233 precisions associated with the memories are equal, the decision landscape takes the shape of a bow-tie pattern. If one 234 stimulus is encoded with higher precision than the other, then the shape of the boundary changes, eventually tending 235 towards the simple threshold on the higher-precision memory.
